resumen: All living organisms are made of **cells**. Cells are so small that we need a **microscope** to **magnify** them.
## Parts of a plant cell
- **Cell wall**: strong and stiff, holds the cell in shape. Made of **cellulose**.
- **Cell membrane**: thin and flexible, lies inside the cell wall, controls what goes in and out.
- **Cytoplasm**: like clear jelly; chemical reactions that keep the cell alive happen here.
- **Nucleus**: controls the activities of the cell.
- **Sap vacuole**: large space filled with **cell sap** (sugars and other substances dissolved in water).
- **Chloroplasts**: where plants make their food (photosynthesis). Green because they contain **chlorophyll**.
- **Mitochondria** (singular: mitochondrion): energy is released from food.
## Microscopes
Parts: eyepiece, coarse and fine focussing knobs, objective lenses (low, medium, high power), stage, mirror.
To look at onion cells: put a thin layer of onion in a drop of water on a slide, lower a **cover slip** without air bubbles, start with the **smallest objective lens**, then focus.
Onion cells are not green because they have no chloroplasts (they grow underground, away from light).
A model of a cell has **strengths** and **limitations** (weaknesses).

resumen: All animals, including you, are made of cells (about 100 trillion in a person).
## Similarities with plant cells
Animal cells also have a **cell membrane**, **cytoplasm**, **mitochondria** and a **nucleus**.
## Differences
Animal cells do **not** have a cell wall, chloroplasts or a large sap vacuole. Their shape is often irregular or round.
## Looking at cheek cells
Rub a cotton bud inside your cheek, rub it on a slide, add a drop of **methylene blue**. It **stains** the cells blue so they are easier to see. Wear **safety glasses**.

resumen: Each kind of cell has a **function** (the job it does). A **specialised** cell has a structure that helps it do its function well: it is **adapted**.
## Specialised animal cells
- **Red blood cell**: carries oxygen. Small, to fit through tiny **capillaries**. Full of the red **pigment haemoglobin**, which carries oxygen. **No nucleus**, leaving more space for haemoglobin.
- **Neurone**: carries **electrical signals** around the body (e.g. from the brain to muscles). Long **axon** for fast signals; **dendrites** collect signals from other nerve cells.
- **Ciliated cell**: has tiny hairs called **cilia** that move. Lines the tubes to the lungs. Other cells make sticky **mucus** that traps dust and bacteria; cilia sweep it up to the mouth.
## Specialised plant cells
- **Root hair cell**: on the outside of roots; **absorbs** water from the soil. Long thin extension. No chloroplasts (no light underground).
- **Palisade cell**: in leaves; makes food by photosynthesis. Lots of **chloroplasts** with chlorophyll, which absorbs energy from sunlight.

resumen: Living things are called **organisms**.
## From cells to organisms
- **Tissue**: a group of similar cells working together to carry out a function. Examples: **onion epidermis**, **ciliated epithelium** (lines the tubes to the lungs).
- **Organ**: a structure made of several different tissues working together. Examples: brain, heart, stomach, muscles; in plants: leaves, roots, flowers.
- **Organ system**: a set of organs working together for the same function, e.g. the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels), digestive, respiratory, skeletal systems.
- A leaf contains an **upper epidermis**, **palisade layer**, **spongy layer** and **lower epidermis**.
## Cell discovery timeline
- 1625 Galileo builds the first microscope.
- 1665 Robert Hooke looks at cork and names the little compartments **cells**.
- 1670 Anton van Leeuwenhoek improves the microscope and sees living cells in pond water.
- 1833 Robert Brown discovers the nucleus in plant cells.
- 1838 Schleiden: all plant tissues are made of cells; Schwann: animal tissues too.
- 1845 Carl Heinrich Braun: cells are the basic unit of all life.
- 1855 Rudolf Virchow: all cells come only from other cells.

resumen: ## States of matter
Everything you can see and feel is **matter**. Scientists sort it into three **states of matter**: **solids**, **liquids** and **gases**. The ways they behave are their **properties**.
- **Solids** keep the same shape and volume. They cannot be **compressed** (squashed) or **poured**.
- **Liquids** take the shape of their container and can be poured. They cannot be compressed. Their volume does not change.
- **Gases** **flow** and fill any closed container. They are very easy to compress, their volume can change and they weigh very little.
## Hypothesis and theory
- A **hypothesis** is a suggestion for an explanation. It is tested with more investigations.
- When a hypothesis has been tested and widely accepted by other scientists, it is a **theory**.
## Particle theory
All matter is made of tiny **particles**, much too small to see.
- **Solid**: fixed pattern, held together strongly, tightly packed. Particles **vibrate** but stay in place.
- **Liquid**: particles touch, held together weakly, can move past one another.
- **Gas**: particles do not touch, are a long way apart and spread out to fill the space.
## Explaining the properties
Matter can only **flow** (be poured) if its particles can **move past one another**. It can only change **volume** if its particles can spread out or move closer together.

- **Solids**: particles very close together, so the volume is hard to make smaller. **Attractive forces** hold the particles together and stop them moving around; they can only **vibrate**. So a solid has a fixed shape and **cannot flow**.

- **Liquids**: particles very close together and touching, so they **cannot be compressed**. The attractive forces are weak enough to let them move past each other but strong enough to hold them together. So liquids **can flow**.

- **Gases**: particles a long way apart, moving quickly in all directions. There are **no attractive forces** between them, so a gas has **no fixed shape or volume**. When you compress a gas, the particles move closer together and it takes up less space.
- A space with **no particles at all** is a **vacuum**. A vacuum contains nothing.
## Modelling particles

A **model** helps us picture something we cannot see. Pupils can act as particles: in regular rows and touching (solid), touching but able to change position (liquid), or spread out and moving (gas). Every model has **strengths** and **weaknesses**.

resumen: ## Changing state
- Ice in a warm place **melts** into liquid water. The temperature at which a solid melts is its **melting point**.
- Water on the ground slowly changes to **water vapour**, an invisible gas. This is **evaporation**. The warmer the water, the faster it evaporates.
- Water heated to **100 °C** **boils** and rapidly turns to **steam**. 100 °C is the **boiling point** of water.
- Water vapour or steam that touches something cold **condenses** back to liquid: **condensation**.
- Liquid water in a freezer **freezes** and becomes ice.
These are **changes of state**.
## Measuring
- **Volume**: use a **measuring cylinder**. The curve at the top is the **meniscus**: read from the **bottom** of it, with your eye **level** with it.
- **Temperature**: use a **thermometer**. The liquid inside expands and rises as it gets hotter. Keep your eye level with the top of the liquid.
## Heating water investigation

Measure 150 cm³ of water, hold the thermometer in the water with a clamp (not touching the bottom of the beaker), heat it and record the temperature every minute until it boils. Plot **time** on the horizontal **axis** and **temperature** on the vertical axis.

resumen: ## Heating

- **Heating solids**: **heat energy is transferred** to the particles. They vibrate more and take up more space, so the solid **expands** (gets bigger). **Attractive forces** still hold them in position.
- **Melting**: the particles vibrate so much that the forces cannot hold them in a fixed pattern. They slide past one another but still touch: a liquid.
- **Boiling**: some liquid particles get enough energy to break the weak attractive forces and escape as gas particles.
## Cooling
- **Condensing**: gas particles have no forces holding them. At a cold surface they lose heat energy to the surface, move less and get closer together: a liquid.
- **Freezing**: heat energy goes from the particles to the surroundings. They move more slowly until they can only vibrate, in a fixed pattern: a solid.

resumen: Water is vital for all living things. Our bodies are made up of at least **60 % water**.

Water on Earth is always moving between rivers, lakes, oceans, the **atmosphere** and the land. It is recycled over and over in a continuous system called the **water cycle**. The Earth has been recycling water for more than **four billion years**: you use the same water as the ancient Greeks and Romans.
## Stages

- **Evaporation**: energy from the **Sun** heats the water in rivers, lakes and oceans. Some particles gain enough energy to break free from the forces holding them and change to a gas: **water vapour**, which moves into the atmosphere.
- **Transpiration**: water evaporates into the atmosphere from **plants**.
- **Condensation**: as water vapour rises it **cools**; its particles lose energy and change back into little droplets of water, forming **clouds**. **Air currents** move the clouds around the world.
- **Precipitation**: when the droplets become too heavy for the air to hold, they fall as **rain**; if they become colder they may form **snow, hail or sleet**.
## Where the water goes
- It collects in rivers and **open water** (large lakes and oceans), then evaporates again.
- On plants it may evaporate from the leaves or trickle down to the ground, where roots take it up.
- Some soaks into soil and rocks as **groundwater** and refills underground stores.
- In cold climates it builds up as snow, ice or glaciers, which melt when it gets warmer.
- Water that flows across the ground into rivers, lakes and oceans is **surface run-off**. Lots of run-off carries soil into rivers, which can become silted up and blocked.

temas.titulo: 2.5 · Atoms, elements and the Periodic Table
resumen: ## Atoms

Over 2000 years ago the Greek philosopher **Democritus** suggested that everything is made of tiny pieces that cannot be cut up any more. He called them **atoms** ('cannot be divided'). Today special microscopes can show atoms, for example in carbon **nanotubes** (nano = very, very small).
## Elements
- **94** types of atom occur naturally; another **24** have been made in laboratories (**118** known elements).
- An **element** is a substance made of just **one kind of atom**: carbon, gold, silver.
- Each type of atom has different properties, so elements have different properties.

- In some elements (e.g. **neon**, a gas) atoms move freely; in most (e.g. **gold** and other metals) they are packed closely; in a few, atoms join into small particles: **oxygen** (2 atoms), **sulfur** (8 atoms).
## The Periodic Table
- Rows are **periods**; columns are **groups**. Across a period, atoms get heavier: hydrogen is the lightest, then helium, then lithium.
- Elements with similar properties are close together: **metals** (yellow boxes) and **non-metals** (blue boxes).
- Each element has a **symbol**: first letter (O), first letter + another (He), or from another language (Na from Latin *natrium*). First letter **upper case**, second **lower case**.

resumen: ## Compounds
- A **compound** is made of more than one type of atom joined tightly together. Joining tightly is called **bonding**.
- Sodium + chlorine → **sodium chloride** (common salt).
- A compound has totally **new properties**: you eat salt, but you would not want to eat sodium or chlorine.
## Naming compounds
- If there is a **metal**, its name comes **first**.
- The **non-metal** name usually changes: sodium chlor**ide**, not sodium chlorine. Two elements → often ends in **-ide**.
- Two elements plus **oxygen** → often ends in **-ate**: calcium carbon**ate** (calcium, carbon, oxygen).
- **Di** = two, **mon/mono** = one: carbon **di**oxide (CO₂), carbon **mon**oxide (CO).
## Formulae
Every compound has a **formula** (plural **formulae**) made of the symbols of its elements. The small number below and to the right says how many atoms of that element; no number means one.
- CaO, CO₂, CO, H₂S, CaCO₃, NaOH
- Careful: **C** is carbon, **Ca** is calcium.
- In a **particle diagram**, different kinds of atom bonded together = compound (H₂O, CO₂, CH₄); O₂ is an element.

resumen: ## Iron and sulfur
- **Iron** is a metal: hard, grey, conducts electricity and is **magnetic**. **Sulfur** is a non-metal: yellow, brittle, does not conduct electricity and is not magnetic.
- **Mixture**: stir iron **filings** and powdered sulfur together. Both keep their properties, so a **magnet** can separate the iron.
- **Compound**: heat the mixture until it glows. The iron and sulfur combine to form **iron sulfide**. A magnet can no longer pull the iron out.
- Safety: safety glasses, don't touch your face, mineral wool in the tube, well-ventilated room.
## Mixtures
- **Pure** means containing only a single substance (pure water is only water).
- A **mixture** is not pure: different kinds of particle mixed, not bonded. They can be elements, compounds or both, and solids, liquids or gases.
- **Air** is a mixture: about **78 % nitrogen**, **21 % oxygen**, 1 % carbon dioxide, argon, water vapour and other gases.

- The **composition** of air varies: water vapour changes with the weather; **natural emissions** (animals and plants respiring) add carbon dioxide; plants making food remove it; burning **fossil fuels** adds it. Long ago there was much less oxygen.
- **Mineral water** is a mixture: **minerals** dissolved in water (a **solution**), about 0.5 g in a litre.
